# Executive summary 

#### Gold: nearing its peak 

After two years of rapid expansion, the gold market surplus dropped to 1,138 tonnes in 2011. This is 21% lower than in 2010, and reflects increased purchases by the official sector and lower scrap supplies alongside a fabrication demand that was largely flat. 



- Although gold has delivered no growth in price terms during the first half of 2012, we expect prices to resume their upward trend in the next six months. However, we believe that the gains for the year as a whole are likely to be moderate.  Overall, we forecast that the gold price will average $1,680/oz in 2012. 



- In 2013, we expect gold’s price rally to falter l

argely because of investors re-evaluating the risks that global financial markets face as well as higher levels of investor fatigue.  In the years beyond 2013, a sustained rise in interest rates and improvement in global economic conditions could prompt investors to intensify liquidation of their long positions in gold. The average gold price over our forecast period is expected to equal $1,603/oz in nominal terms and $1,542/oz in real terms as quotations continue to slip year-on-year to at least 2016. 



- Mine supply is expected to grow steadily throughout our whole outlook period.  However, in an environment of declining prices, the importance of producer hedging could increase. 



- Over the next five years, global gold supply may increase by a net 5% with steady growth witnessed in the 2012-15 period.  In the final year of our outlook, we expect growth to give way to contraction, perhaps of 1.5%, largely because of a sizeable drop in secondary supplies as they respond to lower gold prices. 



- We expect total fabrication demand for gold to get close to its pre-crisis 2007 level by 2016. However, it may need another year or two before the recovery from the effects of the global financial crisis is entirely complete. 



- India and China will remain the world’s two largest markets for gold jewellery for at least another five years.  However, both countries could struggle to maintain their past furious growth over the period.  China is likely to overtake India in 2012 and become the largest gold jewellery market over a full calendar year for the first time.  But India may reclaim its status of the world’s largest gold jewellery market in 2016 when China’s gold jewellery market may experience its first fall in a number of years. 



- Gold fabrication for other applications is unlikely to demonstrate growth this year given the tough economic climate many countries have been facing so far.  The pressure may start to ease in 2013, when we expect gold prices to begin to move lower.

#### Other precious metal markets 

###### Silver 

Weakening economic growth has continued to curtail industrial demand for silver.  Silver’s price has therefore not been immune to the wider sell-off among the base metals and has shed about 15% of its US dollar value during the last three months.  Its fortunes were clearly marked out from gold by the gold:silver price ratio rising from 51-52 to 58-59. 



- Fabrication demand in 2011 slowed more markedly than we previously thought.  Indeed, we now have it slipping by 1-1.5%.  And from a lower base, we now have offtake taking a slower path so that the total is 900 tonnes lower in 2016 than we were quoting last time. 



- The cut to our estimate of mine production in 2011 is minor and we continue to forecast it rising to 27,000 tonnes in 2016.  This assumes that delays to financing slow project development and that

silver’s price fallen by the time that such funding is easier to come by. 



- We continue to believe investor buying will continue to support silver’s price until 2014 and this should prevent project development from rising unchecked.  Nevertheless, weaker fabrication demand could now leave the global surplus running at 5,000 t/y through to 2016. 

###### Platinum 

We still expect platinum’s fundamental surplus to narrow in 2012.  However, its size in absolute terms will be slightly higher than we envisioned in March.  The shift of the market into deficit is now expected only in 2015. 



- Platinum mine output is likely to be lower this year than previously expected largely because of the rising likelihood that supplies from South Africa will post another annual decline. 



- Anticipated weakness in demand from the global glass industry together with constantly increasing volumes of scrap metal may undercut total net fabrication demand in 2012. 

###### Palladium 

As in our March forecast, we expect the palladium market to remain oversupplied in 2012 on both the fundamental and final levels. If shipments from Russian state stocks halt in 2014, as expected, the market may then swing back into a deficit on both levels. 



- Net demand is likely to take another little retracement this year before it resumes its upward trend.  Another surge in supplies of metal recovered from end-of-life vehicles, albeit of a smaller size than in 2011, should outweigh the moderate growth in underlying fabrication demand in 2012.  Increased scrap availability is meanwhile boosting this year’s supply. 



- The decline in primary production of palladium is likely to be steeper in 2012 than we anticipated in March.  Alongside our expectations of lower output from South Africa, we have downgraded our production estimates for Russian and North American palladium miners.

# Chapter 1 Gold 

#### 1.  Summary 

The year 2011 marked a decade since the gold market balance shifted into fundamental surplus.  The size of the surplus, however, did not expand last year as it did in 2010 and most notably in 2009, but actually dropped by 21% to 1,138 tonnes. 

One key factor behind this radical end to expansion was an actual loss of one of the important sources of gold supply – official sector sales, which primarily represent the actions of central banks in various countries.  The official sector was a net seller for six consecutive years between 2002 and 2007 before turning into a net buyer in 2008 and 2009.  In 2010, it changed again, but the scale of sales was insignificant.  And, after this short break, central banks returned with even greater appetite for gold

in 2011.  Their net purchases of slightly over 400 tonnes had a significant negative impact on the overall level of global gold supply last year.  Prior to 2011, sales of gold by central banks averaged approximately 300 t/y.  In some years, the sector even contributed of up to 20% of global gold supply. 

With this source of supply gone, global gold supply reduced in volume as none of the other three major sources were able to fill the void.  Specifically, gold miners, which had been ramping up output for three years, managed to increase their contribution by only 38 tonnes year-on-year or 1.5%.  An additional 12 tonnes were brought to the market due to the first net expansion of the global gold producer hedge book in more than ten years, this contrasting with a 121 tonnes contraction of producers’ hedges in 2010.  And the additional 171 tonnes that these two sources supplied to the gold market in 2011 was partly offset by a fall in secondary output where year-on-year volumes declined by 58 tonnes.  Adding in the negative sales from the official sector, world gold supply fell by 7.5% last year to a total of 3,892 tonnes. 

It was only because fabrication demand was also weak in 2011 that the market surplus did not shrink by even more.  Fairly speaking, the overall impact that this part of the supply-demand equation had on the change in the size of market balance was muted; total fabrication demand fell by 0.5% last year to 2,754 tonnes.  Lacklustre demand for jewellery was the largest absolute driver of this decline.  The total drop would have been more substantial had jewellery’s fall not been offset by brisk growth in demand for gold coins which jumped by 13% year-on-year.  This area of offtake fully recouped the losses incurred in the 2010, with annual demand hitting a new record of 240 tonnes. ###### irreversible downward trend. 

In 2012, we expect the market balance to expand again on the back of the resumption of growth in global gold supply driven by rising mine output and a recovery in gold recycling in response to higher gold prices.  In part for the same reason, and partly because of the global economic slowdown, fabrication demand for gold is expected to shrink further this year, leaving a significant amount of metal for the investment sector to clear. 

As such, although we expect gold prices to resume their upward trend in the next six months, we believe that the net gain for this year as a whole is likely to be moderate.  Overall, we forecast that the gold price will average $1,680/oz in 2012, with a $1,710/oz average in the second half.

#### 2.  Gold fabrication demand 

###### 2.1  Summary 

Our definition of fabrication demand includes demand for physical gold in the form of jewellery, coins and medallions, most of which is partly driven by the metal’s investment appeal.  True industrial uses are limited mainly to electronics, dental and a handful of minor applications. 

In 2012, we expect global fabrication demand to fall for the second consecutive year.  As in 2011, lacklustre demand for jewellery is likely to be the largest absolute driver of this decline. Record high gold prices in India as a result of rupee devaluation combined with restrictive measures that the Indian government has taken to curb domestic gold demand will almost certainly suppress gold use in jewellery and medallion fabrication, as well as in some other applications in this key gold market.  The vast size of the Indian gold market and high price sensitivity of local gold consumers means that, even if a small percentage of buyers decide to postpone their purchase of gold jewellery, it would result in a significant drop in actual physical demand.  Admittedly, China’s growing love for luxury goods, including gold jewellery, will cushion the fall in demand from India, but we do not expect it to entirely offset it.

###### 2.2  Jewellery fabrication 

###### **Introduction** 

Our statistics for jewellery consumption measure the gold content of new, carat jewellery and watches and are allocated between countries in line with final sales.  They exclude the gold contained in second-hand jewellery, gold-plated jewellery (which is included in industrial fabrication), coins and bars that are used as jewellery, and the part-exchange of existing for new pieces.  Global jewellery demand is driven by a combination of affordability and desirability.

Fabricators’ purchases of new and scrap gold will fluctuate around our totals for jewellery sales as manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers all adjust their stocks. 

In the developed world, gold jewellery is a luxury and d

iscretionary adornment purchase rather than an investment.  Thus, it is positively related to disposable income and negatively related to price.  Before the latest economic downturn, these two factors more or less balanced out, and developed countries accounted for a fairly stable 22-25% of global jewellery consumption.  More recently, however, both absolute demand and its market share have collapsed such that only 9% of last year’s global purchases were located in Western Europe, North America and Japan. 

Developing countries, most notably India, China, the rest of Asia and the Middle East, now account for the vast bulk of global jewellery offtake.  In these countries, there can be a significant overlap between the adornment and savings and investment motives in jewellery purchases.  The jewellery bought in developing countries is typically of high purity (22 carat), non-branded and sold by weight at a relatively small margin over its contained metal cost. Consequently, changes in the gold price feed quickly through into that of finished jewellery. And consumers in these markets tend to be very price sensitive.  While there has been some move towards Western style products (most often imported and sold by piece) in many developing markets, this generally still comprises a small percentage of total sales. 

Factors influencing gold demand in developing countries include the gold price level and volatility (in US dollar and local currency terms), gold price expectations, cultural and social factors, disposable incomes, investor confidence, competition for discretionary spending from other luxury goods and services, design trends, tax and tariff changes on raw materials and finished products, the quality and price of competing finished jewellery products and any preference for alternative gold investment vehicles. 

However, it would be wrong to suppose that these factors interact identically in every country.  In India, for example, gold (and silver) jewellery is mainly viewed as a safe and portable vehicle for savings.  Money flows into the precious metal markets are therefore mainly a function of income, although the tonnages that these money flows will purchase are inversely related to local prices, while the choice of which metal to buy will also be influenced by the ratios of different precious metal quotations.  At the other extreme, jewellery purchases in China and the Middle East have a very high investment motive, and may actually be encouraged by a clearly appreciating price.

One should note that the growth in gold output witnessed in 2011, 2010 and 2009 was the result of efforts that began about a decade ago.  With the price of gold spiralling downwards in the late 1980s and 1990s, most gold miners struggled for survival as their margins virtually vanished.  This in turn significantly undercut their exploration and development budgets.  On top of that, during the global technology boom in the late 1990s and early 2000s, gold stocks were largely unpopular with the global investment community, and this made raising capital nearly impossible for the miners.  As a result, for many years, gold mines were depleting at a faster pace than their replacements were coming on stream.  In other words, the big production decline between 2003 and 2008 was the result of many years of neglect, and meant that gold companies could not take full advantage of the fact that gold demand and consequently gold price have risen every year since 2001. 

Eventually, though, rising gold prices induced investors to turn their eyes on gold mining companies again.  The inflow of fresh capital resulted in a major increase in exploration spending and mine development which, in turn, led to new discoveries and brought new gold mines on stream.  However, it typically takes between 10 and 15 years to get a decent-sized mine from discovery to commercial production, which means that many of the gold mines being brought into production today are tapping mineralisation that was discovered many years ago. Interestingly, even with 2011’s all-time high, gold’s annual production growth since 2001, when the current gold bull run commenced, has averaged a miniscule 0.3%, meaning that effectively there has been no production growth over the last 11 years.

###### **Forecast production** 

Until recently, the long lag time between investment and output has been masking gold miners’ response to higher prices.  But, having hit record high levels of output in the last two years, the global gold mining industry appears to be reversing a decade-long trend of weak and unstable production. 

Indeed, thanks to higher gold prices, gold miners are extremely motivated to increase gold output even despite a range of obstacles they continue to face.  These include declining ore grades, rising costs, increased government and environmental regulations, and reserves that are increasingly difficult to access, not to mention a shortage of skilled technical specialists. Although addressing these challenges is not a quick and easy task, at current price levels, which are well above the cost of production, gold miners can still overcome escalating costs relatively comfortably and therefore risk re-starting operations at some mines which had to be mothballed earlier for economic reasons or even bring into production projects that would have been rejected as too expensive just a couple of years ago.  Also, more gold production is scheduled to come on stream during the next few years as investments made earlier in the mining cycle translate into greater output. 

Importantly, the miners are not stopping laying the groundwork for future expansion and keep investing in exploration and mine development as they try to make up for lost time. According to the _Metals Economics Group_ , the estimated total spending on nonferrous metals exploration in 2011 reached a record $18.2 billion, up around 50% f

rom $12.1 billion in 2010. Noteworthy, gold projects received the largest portion of investment, accounting for about half of the global exploration budget for the second year in a row. The sheer scale of exploration dollars being injected into the gold mining industry makes us think that the output trajectory for at least the next five years is likely to be higher. Underpinning this, exploration spending dedicated to early-stage work has been at historically low levels for the last three years, while late-stage and mine-site budgets have been receiving a higher proportion of spending. This reflects the desire of gold miners to push nearterm production forward, even if this comes at the expense of future output. However, as we mentioned before, a long period of time is needed to advance fresh discoveries to production and therefore too much focus on late-stage spending today may eventually have negative consequences for gold mine supply in a few years time. Most of this scrap comes from recycled jewellery, but some emanates from other old or discarded fabricated products. Unlike mine production, scrap supply is influenced by mainly short-term factors, perhaps the most important of which are price and price volatility. The official sector covers gold bullion reserves held by central banks and similar bodies as well as by supranational bodies such as the IMF, BIS and ECB.  Their combined gold holdings totalled 30,335 tonnes at the end of last year, down from a mid-1960s peak of approaching 40,000 tonnes.  As a legacy of the gold standard, post-war period and Bretton Woods, a number of Western central banks and the IMF have substantial holdings of gold as a proportion of their total reserves.  The USA has the largest gold holdings in the world, which is consistent with its position as the issuer of the world’s primary reserve currency. 

Between the late 1980s and 2007, the official sector was a net, annual seller of gold, with disposals largely from European central banks more than matching additions to reserves in the developing world.  Since 1999, the bulk of the former have taken place under the framework of Central Bank Gold Agreements.  The latter have been less co-ordinated across regions or through time.

Mining companies sometimes sell forward a portion of their future production to a financial institution in order to gain finance for a new mining project or to guarantee future sales receipts. A producer may choose to undertake hedging activity to provide protection against an expected decline in the gold price.  Conversely, if the gold price is expected to rise, it may choose to unwind its existing hedge book to gain exposure to the benefits of that increase.  A mining company’s gold hedge book comprises the total set of positions it holds as gold forward sales, options and other derivative instruments.  Changes to these positions have an impact on the spot physical gold market, typically through gold leasing arrangements. 

There are three main parties involved in a basic gold hedge contract: the producer; a bullion bank, which acts as the producer’s dealer; and a central bank.  To place a hedge, the producer advises its dealer tha

t it wishes to forward sell, for example, one tonne of metal.  The dealer then borrows this amount from a central bank (paying a leasing fee), which it immediately sells into the spot market, agreeing to return the one tonne by a certain date.  The proceeds from this sale are then placed in a high-yielding cash account (subtracting the dealer’s fee and the leasing fee on the borrowed gold), usually generating a premium for the producer.  The producer is obliged to return the one tonne of gold to the bullion bank by the pre-agreed date.  At the time of implementation, the bullion bank’s borrowing of the gold and selling it into the spot market increases the supply of gold to the market.  However, when the gold is returned, usually by delivering mine production from the producer’s account, supply reaching the market is correspondingly constrained.  Hedging activity therefore represents an acceleration of supply to the market, but the overall balance of supply and demand is maintained over the lifetime of the transaction. 

The 1990s were largely characterised by unrelenting downward pressure on the gold price, which led to steadily increasing levels of hedging undertaken by producers who were seeking revenue protection from further declines.  In 1995, hedging had a particularly noticeable impact, reaching 475 tonnes and thereby accounting for about 13% of total supply. 

Producers’ reversal in hedging policies dates back to the beginning of the current bull cycle in 2000-01.  When the gold price had made an abrupt change of direction and started to climb, many hedged producers were caught off-guard and were unable to take advantage of soaring spot prices.  On the back of this, 2000 was the first year since the late 1970s when the global producer hedge book did not expand.  There has since been a protracted period of de-hedging, in which producers have both delivered into and prematurely closed out their hedge contracts. This has been accomplished either by bullion purchases from the market, delivered to the bullion bank, or through delivering their own production into contracts before they mature.  Dehedging hit a record of 444 tonnes in 2007, removing 12% from total gold supply.  Expectations for higher gold prices and mining company investors’ associated anti-hedging sentiment were the chief reasons for this. 

Prior to 2000, producer hedging was thus a significant supply component in the gold market whereas, post-2000, hedging activity acted to tighten the fundamental balance.  Having said this, the pace of producer buybacks has slowed markedly in recent years, as a greatly diminished global hedge book has left producers with little in the way of hedge positions to close out. As producer de-hedging slowly fades, an important constraint on available supply has gradually been removed from the market.

###### 4.1  Recent price developments 

In 2011, gold posted its tenth consecutive year of annual price gains – at $1,571/oz its average for the year was 28% higher than in 2010.  This was gold’s second strongest annual performance in relative terms during this bull run, beaten only by the rise of 36% registered in 2006, but that was from a much lower base.  In absolute terms, last year set the record, with prices rising by nearly $346/oz. 

Not every investor managed to profit from this gain though, as gold prices proved to be very volatile.  Having started the year at $1,388/oz, gold initially weakened as economic sentiment temporarily improved, with the gold price hitting its low for the year of $1,319/oz in late January.  From there, it started to move higher as the global political and economical situation continued to worsen.  The upward move accelerated in July as concerns grew about the outcome of negotiations between the US Administration and Congress over the country’s debt ceiling ahead of its deadline on 2 August.  Although both parties eventually came to an agreement and the ceiling was raised, market confidence in the ability of the US officials to perform their duties efficiently was

severely dented; on 5 August, the US credit rating was downgraded to less than AAA for the first time in its history.  As the US dollar, one of gold’s major competitors as a safe haven, was taking a hit, the price of the precious metal exploded to new nominal highs. 

Meanwhile, on the other side of the Atlantic, Europe was trying to solve its own financial conundrum as the mounting sovereign debt problems raised worries about a double dip in the region’s economic activity.  As the euro weakened, the Swiss National Bank intervened in early September and set a ceiling for the Swiss franc at 1.20 to the euro in an attempt to prevent its economy from being dragged into recession by the strength of its currency.  With another safehaven asset effectively off their radar, investors flocked into gold anticipating imminent financial Armageddon.  As a result, the metal reached an intraday high of $1,920/oz on 6 September. 

Shortly after the IMF expressed its concerns about the future prospects for the global economy in its Global Financial Stability report in mid-September, worries over the inevitability of another, perhaps even larger, global recession unnerved investors in virtually all financial markets.  And this led to a period of risk aversion along with widespread asset liquidation as investors raced for cash.  The massive size of this liquidation sparked a wave of margin calls leaving many investors and funds in desperate need for cash to meet their financial obligations. In order to raise this money, many decided to dump gold which is a great source of liquidity during the tight times.  Gold prices fell from their record peak and, as the US dollar firmed later in the year on further euro woes, it slipped back to end 2011 at $1,574.5/oz, only 13% above where it started the year. 

Considerably weakened after the heavy beating which took place during the last few months of 2011, gold started 2012 on a sound note as initially bargain hunters and later other investors, induced by the renewed prospects of the third round of quantitative easing and promises by US officials to maintain a low-interest rate environment until at least 2014, pushed the price of gold to a year-to-date high of $1,781/oz in late February. At the end of 2011, platinum looked very week, but some concerns about electricity and primary mine supply from South Africa, where national electricity utility Eskom warned of possible power shortages and Impala Platinum’s Rustenburg operations were paralysed by an unofficial strike, lifted sentiment in January and pushed the platinum price to a year-to-date high of $1,729/oz on 23 February. 

In the turmoil that followed the Federal Reserve’s comments at the end of February suggesting that QE3 might not yet happen, all four major precious metals prices plunged. Indeed, platinum briefly recaptured a price premium over gold around mid-March for the first time since September 2011. 

While platinum had been trading below gold, many investors followed a sell-gold-buyplatinum strategy betting on the re-establishment of platinum’s traditional price premium.  And this had provided a little stronger support for this precious metal.  However, as soon as the strategy had borne fruit, investor interest evaporated and platinum lost much of its momentum. As a result, in the second half of the month, platinum weakened to a greater extent than gold and moved back into a discount. 

Renewed fears about the EU economy in combination with negative news from the European automotive market and reports of a slowdown in the Chinese economy continued to drag the platinum price lower during April and May. ###### Net fabrication demand for platinum may drop before things start to improve 

Net global fabrication demand for platinum in 2011 stood at 5,590 koz, according to the latest data compiled by _Johnson Matthey_ in March _._ This is 115 koz or 2% lower than the company envisioned back in November.  Despite the downward revision, net platinum consumption by industrial consumers still posted a positive growth of 3.1% from 5.420 koz in 2010, continuing its recovery from 2009.  As _Johnson Matthey_ is our primary statistical source, our own (gross) consumption estimates incorporate similar changes. 

_Johnson Matthey’s_ downgrading has affected demand estimates for nearly all industrial applications with the steepest drops seen in the jewellery and automotive sectors.  As a result, net demand in these sectors is now estimated to have fallen by 105 koz and 100 koz respectively from 2010.  However, these drops were not caused by any weakening of underlying demand – at the gross level year-on-year growth was actually registered in every industrial sector – but was rather a result of a higher than expected pick-up in platinum scrap supplies, driven principally by higher returns of end-of-life vehicle catalysts and old platinum jewellery pieces. Specifically, recycling of autocatalysts grew by 13% to 1,225 koz, while jewellery recycling rose by 10% to 810 koz. 

If last year’s growth in platinum recovery from autocatalysts was of little surprise as it had already become a part of a long and well-established trend (many cars scrapped in 2011 were manufactured in early 2000s when diesel-powered vehicles were gaining popularity and when Euro 3 came into force requiring higher platinum loadings), then the change in _Johnson Matthey’s_ view on the recycling of platinum jewellery was something we found particularly interesting.  The fact is that in its November review, the company did not expect any increases in platinum jewellery recycling.  Quite the opposite, the level of recycling was projected to fall by 15% to 690 koz.  In our view, the reason for such a significant revision could be some overordering of platinum stock by retailers and wholesalers when the metal started trading at a discount to gold in the third quarter of last year.  The jewellery trade might then have tried to capitalise on what it expected soon to be a re-establishment of platinum’s price premium over gold.  When, after a few weeks, it had become clear that such strategy was not bearing fruit, some jewellers will have been forced to liquidate excessive stock of platinum by selling it back into the market.  As a result, net demand from this source fell by 0.9% against its 2010 level.

they bought 3,105 koz of platinum against 3,075 koz one year earlier.  The pace of the annual growth, however, slowed significantly and totalled just 1% compared with 41% posted in 2010.  This is perhaps not surprising as in many regions demand for new vehicles, particularly in the light duty sector, was badly affected by growing concerns over the state of health of the global economy and shaky consumer sentiment.  In addition, purchasing of platinum by Japanese car manufacturers dropped as they lowered output in the wake of the natural disaster which hit the nation in March of last year.  On top of that, the trend to introduce more palladium into diesel catalysts remained intact; according to _Johnson Matthey_ , palladium now accounts for some 30% of PGM demand in this sector, with some 50:50 Pt:Pd catalysts already in use. 

The negative effects of these factors, however, were fully offset by the strong growth in the purchasing of platinum in the heavy duty diesel sector.  As fleet operators, primarily in North America, returned to the market following the recession, large truck manufacturers increased platinum purchases by 27% from 400 koz in 2010 to 515 koz last year. 

The outlook for platinum demand in the auto sector in 2012 is mixed as one might expect with downbeat Eurozone sentiment weighing on automotive demand.  Because of deepening recession in large parts of Europe, regional car sales in the first five months of this year were nearly 8% lower than in the same period of 2011.  The outlook for the European economy has continued to darken and we maintain our negative stance on demand for platinum from local vehicle producers which we expect to fall this year by approximately 7% to 1,360 koz. 

The outlook for diesel vehicle demand (and hence for platinum) in the markets outside Europe remains more positive.  So far this year, diesel car sales have been very strong not only in Japan, where the economy is recovering quickly from last year’s disaster, but also in India, where diesel cars now account for about 40% of total sales.  And yet, the real story is the US market where we might be seeing the start of a golden era for diesel-powered cars; clean diesel sales were up 35% in the first quarter of 2012 over 2011 Q1 on the back of rising demand for more fuel-efficient cars spurred by higher fuel prices.  That said, at around 3%, the market share of diesel engines in the USA is still way below that in Europe where diesel vehicles occupy 52% of the local car market.  However, according to the latest estimates by the Bosch Group, the country will see diesels grab 10% of the national market by 2015, five years earlier than it had previously expected. 

Meanwhile, for the first time, diesel engines’ share of the passenger car market in the UK climbed from 49.4% in the first four months of 2011 to 50.8% in the first four months of 2012. The upcoming introduction of Euro 6 engine emission legislation, which begins to come into force in January 2

013, will also prompt the use of more platinum to treat NOx emissions from both heavy and light duty vehicles throughout Europe.  Even there, the outlook for automotive sector demand for platinum is therefore healthier than might be thought by simply looking at depressing European car sales figures.  For this reason, our forecast for platinum demand from this sector has remained largely unchanged.

###### Global platinum mine supply is under pressure as platinum miners are struggling to increase output 

Platinum mine output is likely to be lower this year than we anticipated in March largely because of the rising likelihood that supplies from South Africa will post another annual decline.  The industrial relations climate in that country remains m

ore than challenging and has led to further mine supply disruptions. 

Since our latest publication in March, South Africa’s platinum mining industry has continued to suffer from strike action.  During the March-April period, a three week long strike was seen at Modikwa, a joint venture between ARM and Anglo American Platinum.  The strike continued until the 10th of April and resulted in a loss of approximately 20 koz of PGMs.  In mid-May, disruption was again seen at Impala Platinum’s troubled Rustenburg mine where supporters of the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) and the Association of Mineworkers and Construction Union (AMCU) clashed over dominance.  As a result, some 6 koz of platinum were added to the production lost from the Impala industrial unrest earlier this year when a strike reportedly cost the company 146 koz of metal. 

We expect further losses of platinum production due to strike action this year particularly given that the NUM will hold its leadership elections in June.  Additionally, other factors such as frequent Section 54 closures and steadily escalating operational expenses incurred by local

###### The platinum market keeps tightening 

We have revised our March estimates for this year’s platinum mine supply and fabrication demand downwards in order to reflect the challenges that platinum market continues to face. After receiving a heavy beating in the second half of 2011, the metal started 2012 in an upbeat mood with prices climbing on the back of a combination of supply concerns and improved auto sales in the USA.  At the end of February, quotations reached $722/oz, representing a 9% gain since the start of the year. 

Since that point and until early April, however, palladium was primarily on a downward trend driven lower by news about fading economic growth in China, aggravated by a large fall in domestic sales of passenger cars, and receding hopes of US quantitative easing. 

In April, palladium made an attempt to decouple from the otherwise depressed precious metals complex, drawing support from another bout of good auto data from the USA where pent-up demand and cheaper credit led to a rise in car sales.  The fact that Nymex cut margins on palladium contracts also boosted buying sentiment.  However, even this more bullish mood was not enough for palladium to recapture the psychologically important level of $700/oz. 

Furthermore, the positive sentiment did not last long though as bullishness was sapped from the market in early May by a combination of a soft euro, weak economic data, heighten risk aversion, and heavy losses among other precious metals.  As a result, palladium prices plunged by over 13% to $590/oz by the middle of the month.  In the second half, however, a rising gold price and positive news about the Chinese government preparing another stimulus programme to support national economic growth proved supportive for palladium and helped to push its price back above $600/oz. 

In mid-June, palladium rallied to a high of $634/oz. At the end of the month, palladium again found itself below the 600/oz mark following the general market reaction to German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s decisive resistance to the use of so-called Euro-bonds and therefore decreasing confidence in the prospect of an early resolution of the ongoing euro crisis.

###### Net fabrication demand for palladium is taking a step back, but the long-term upward trend remains intact 

According to the data recently published by _Johnson Matthey,_

palladium fabrication demand was generally healthy during 2011; gross metal consumption increased by 4.3% or 375 koz to a total of 9,015 koz compared with 8,640 koz consumed in 2010.  It is worth noting that this final figure is 1% or 90 koz lower than the company’s preliminary projection of 9,105 koz made in September. 

Last year’s growth in demand was primarily driven by increases in gross consumption by the automotive and chemical sectors.  Gross automotive demand increased by 8.1% to 6,030 koz (up 2% from the September estimate), driven by strong growth in many emerging markets, a rebound in sales in North America and the growing penetration of palladium in the European diesel sector (where palladium now represents 30% of precious metal used).  Meanwhile, new chemicals plants brought on stream in China boosted purchases of palladium by the global chemical industry by 20% to 445 koz (down 2% from the September estimate).  In contrast, demand for the metal from the electronics industry softened by 2.1% to 1,380 koz as substitution with cheaper base metal alloys continued to take place.  That said, _Johnson Matthey_ had a different view in September – it expected demand to grow by 5% to 1,485 koz.  However, it has changed the final annual figure to reflect a drop in metal demand after the floods in Thailand battered the global electronics industry in October last year. 

In the jewellery sector, a combination of higher prices and waning interest in palladium from jewellery manufacturers, particularly in China, continued to depress demand last year.  Overall, gross palladium demand fell from 595 koz in 2010 to 505 koz in 2011 with demand weakening in every region.  This final figure is 7.3% below of what _Johnson Matthey_ envisioned in its September review, perhaps as a reflection of stronger demand for platinum, its closest competitor, which was trading at an unusual discount to gold in the final quarter of 2011. 

If we look at net demand, we see a somewhat different picture, however.  Along with downward revisions for the gross palladium demand in electrical, chemical, dental, and other applications, _Johnson Matthey_ has raised its 2011 figure for autocatalyst recycling which jumped by 10% to 1,655 koz from a total of 1,505 koz as was reported in its previous review. In combination, these changes outweighed the growth (even though it has also been upgraded) in gross autocatalyst demand and pushed the total net figure for the year down by 3% from 6,575 koz seen in September to 6,375 koz in March<sup>*</sup> .  Meanwhile, on a year-on-year basis, total net fabrication demand dropped by nearly 2% from where it stood in 2010. 

According to _Johnson Matthey_ , latest data for platinum demand in most other industrial applications for 2011 are much closer to the figures we were using as a basis for forecasting last time.

Having incorporated all the recent changes, we maintain our positive outlook for palladium, and expect gross consumption to continue to grow over the next five years.  While many of the vital for palladium offtake, emerging car markets are struggling to maintain last year’s growth rates (including those of China and India), continued growth in North American car and truck sales should keep palladium demand on an upward trend this year too.  Based on JD Power’s global vehicle production forecasts, we expect consumption to continue to grow in the years ahead, even though a repetition of 2010’s strong growth performance is highly unlikely. 

Demand for palladium from the chemical sector should be supported by strong demand for plastics from China while the global electronics sector should use more metal to satisfy pent-up requirements following the recovery from the floods in Thailand.  Against this, dental demand will continue to shrink by a few percentage points each year in the light of long-term improvements in the quality of global dental care and competition from other materials used for dental treatment.  There is, however, a chance that imposition of austerity measures in a growing number of countries may drive dental demand lower more quickly. 

In contrast, net demand is likely to take another little retracement this year before it resumes its upward trend.  Another surge in supplies of metal recovered from end-of-life vehicles, albeit of a smaller size than in 2011, should outweigh the moderate growth in underlying fabrication demand in 2012.  As such, we expect total net fabrication demand to drop by 1.4% to 6,285 koz this year from 6,375 koz in 2011.  By 2016, however, it is forecast to have grown by 39% and total 8,735 koz driven by the global economic recovery, car sales expansion and tightening emission standards that will result in heavier loadings of palladium for autocatalysts.

###### A twisted path towards the balancing point 

According to our recently updated numbers for supply and demand, the palladium market was in oversupply by 1,790 koz last year.  It is 15% higher than we anticipated in March. Although our estimates of last year’s investment demand for palladium and the size of the sales from the Russian star stocks were largely in line with _Johnson Matthey’s_ recently released figures, the company’s downward revision of the volumes consumed by industrial users of this metal means that an additional 231 koz of pa

lladium failed to find any final industrial consumer and were added to the surplus instead. As in our March forecast, we expect the palladium market to remain oversupplied this year on both the fundamental and final levels by perhaps 93 koz and 228 koz respectively. Unlike in 2011, the difference between these two figures is very low due to our expectation that only 135 koz of palladium will be supplied from Russian state stocks in 2012, with this being the smallest shipment of metal from this source during the last five years. It is worth noting here that, without the benefit of Russian stockpile exports, the palladium market would have been in deficit for most of the past 10 years. In 2010, the absence of stockpile sales would have pushed the market deeper into deficit, and in 2011 the substantial surplus would have been reduced considerably without stockpile sales. As mentioned in previous issues of our _Precious Metals Quarterly_ , in October 2011, news reports suggested that Gokhran would sell 135 koz of palladium in 2012 and the same volume CRU International Limited confidential Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 Palladium 131 again in 2013 before its stocks become entirely exhausted. In the first five months of this year, imports of palladium into Switzerland from Russia totalled nearly 67 koz. Some of this material is likely to have come from current mine production, but the general market assumption is that the bulk of it is from Russian state stocks. At current levels, the volumes exported so far are not inconsistent with the indications given in the media and, if these estimations eventually hold true, this would lead to lower supplies in 2014 and may potentially swing the palladium market back into a deficit on both the fundamental and final levels which then may grow rapidly in the 2015-16 period, driven in particular by the recovery in the US auto industry and continued growth in the BRIC nations’ auto industries. Although we remain positive over palladium’s medium to long fundamentals, it is clear that, after a relatively good start to this year, the global economy has been struggling and that demand from industrial and automotive customers may be lower than we expected in March. To reflect this, we have lowered our price forecast for calendar 2012 to $710/oz as well as downgraded our expectations for the four years beyond. Now, we expect the real price of palladium to average $876/oz during the course of our outlook. #### 1.  Risks mount in the Eurozone and China 

The Eurozone is back where it was at the end of 2011, with the added burden of greatly amplified political uncertainty. Meanwhile the Eurozone ex Germany wants to tilt its policy mix more towards growth, but Germany is unlikely to agree to more deficit financing.  So policy changes are likely to be more about rhetoric than substance in the short term, and yield incremental benefits at most.  Thus the main uncertainties are less to do wi

th whether Greece defaults, but more to do with how and when.  A make or break debt repayment is due on 20 August, so the moment of truth is getting closer.

## 2.  Regional developments 

###### 2.1  The Americas: USA a bastion of (modest) growth 

Compared with the Eurozone the USA is a bastion of growth, albeit modest growth.  As expected GDP expanded at a decelerating rate in the first quarter, by 2.2% annualised quarteron-quarter, down from 3% in the final three months of 2011.  Consumption made the biggest contribution, followed by stock building.  The majority of high frequency data indicate that growth is holding up, despite the headwinds from across the Atlantic, much as we expect it to, and as a result we have held our forecast fairly steady this month.  But the outlook is not without its risks, and these may be a little more acute now. 

Activity fluctuates from month to month, but the underlying trend remains positive. Industrial production increased by 1.1% month-on-month in April, following a more volatile performance in the preceding two months.  As a result the three month on three month rate of output growth slowed to a still healthy 7.5% annualised from almost 10% in March.  The April performance lifted the capacity utilisation rate to 79.2%, its highest reading in four years, and only one percentage point shy of its long-run average.  Manufacturing output increased by 0.6%, led by another solid gain in vehicle production.  What is more the Institute of Supply Management’s manufacturing index is signalling further modest output growth in the near term. But modest is all it will be – core orders for durable goods excluding aircraft were flat monthon-month in March, signalling meagre times ahead for some sectors. 

Although domestic demand is expanding at a moderate pace, US industry is being helped by improvements in competitiveness versus most other developed economies and China.  As a result two thirds of US manufacturers have moved facilities in the last two years, and the USA has been the top destination to relocate to.  Looking out to 2013, however, the effects of weak demand for US exports this year, in particular in the Eurozone, is likely to detract from output growth as firms subsequently reduce their inventories. 

More encouraging still, housing starts picked up in April after falling in February and March, by 2.6% month-on-month to an annualised rate of 717,000 units.  The upturn was led by a surge in the construction of apartments for rental, because so many would-be first time buyers are opting to rent at present as they prefer to pay down their student loans before saving for a deposit.  It will be many quarters before construction makes the sort of contribution to GDP growth we grew accustomed to prior to the financial crisis, but because activity is growing from a very low base the sector is starting to recover strongly on trend measures: residential construction spending in the first quarter rose at an annual rate of 19%, and the dearth of properties to let is likely to fuel activity further.  Certainly, house prices measured by the CaseShiller index stabilised in Ma

rch, after 10 months of falls. 

Nonetheless the recovery remains fundamentally modest in nature and that is most evident in the labour market.  The USA created only 115,000 net new non-farm jobs in April.  This was the slowest rate of job formation in six months, and a significant deceleration from the rate around the turn of the year.  The unemployment rate edged lower to 8.1% from 8.2% in March, but that was thanks to the participation rate falling back to a 30 year low.  Critically the jobs market is too fragile to make inroads into long-term unemployment to any significant extent.

###### 2.2  Europe: less whether Greece defaults, more how/when 

The prospect of a disorderly Greek default and possible exit from the Eurozone has intensified following the results of the Greek general election on 6 May, which saw an inconclusive result with a strong representation of anti-bailout parties. The financial consequences of this political stalemate have already started manifesting themselves in rising Spanish and Italian bond yields, and a slow motion bank run in Cyprus and elsewhere on the Eurozone’s periphery.  Meanwhile, France’s new Socialist president, Franзois Hollande, has pledged to prioritise growth over austerity.  However, his plans are likely to face stiff opposition from Angela Merkel, who is determined to force the periphery to stick to their strict spending plans.  Germany represents the biggest upside surprise to our forecast this month, where activity rose by much more than expected in the first quarter of 2012.  However this was countered by an even more recessionary periphery.

Elevated inventories mean that already falling prices are likely to weaken further, significantly boosting affordability given that average urban incomes are rising by close to 15%. 

While investment in residential real estate will slow further, we expect investment in transport infrastructure to rally as approval and funding for new projects comes through. Investment in the power sector has already turned the corner with an increase of 19.0% so far this year fol

lowing a rise of only 3.8% in 2011.  Having been a drag on growth in the second half of 2011, infrastructure investment will make a positive contribution as we move into the second half of this year. 

One of the positive aspects of last month’s data was that inflation fell to 3.4% from 3.6%, led lower by food prices.  We expect inflation to slow further due to base effects and a lagged response to slower economic growth, reaching a trough in the summer.  Not only does the more favourable inflation backdrop give space for policy easing, it is also helping the authorities reform prices further, with residential electricity tariffs to be increased from June.  Our forecast is for inflation to average 3.1% this year, rising to 3.7% next year and 4.0% thereafter; we see higher medium-term inflation as inevitable as labour shortages push up wages and as administered prices are increased to better reflect the costs of provision. 

Due to the disappointing April activity data we have edged our GDP growth forecast for this year down to 8.2% from 8.3%.  We still expect economic recovery to develop in the second half of the year and carry over into stronger growth in 2013, which we peg at 8.8%.  These forecasts are conditional, however, on the Eurozone containing its debt crisis – failure to do so poses the key downside risk to our projections.  The Chinese government is in the fortunate position of having leeway to ease both monetary and fiscal policy to counter an economic shock and we would expect it to do so.  However, the government would be unlikely to launch a stimulus package akin to that seen at the onset of the financial crisis.  Thus GDP growth would be weaker than in our base case, with 7% a plausible lower limit.  An economic shock would alter the profile of our forecasts into the medium term but not our underlying story – trend GDP growth will slow into the medium term for structural reasons and sub-8% growth will become the norm. 

The Japanese economy appears to be stalling again after rebounding in the first three months of 2012.  Economic growth in the first quarter of 1.0% quarter-on-quarter was driven by a 1.1% quarter-on-quarter increase in private consumption, in particular of durable goods which climbed 7.4%.  Private consumption accounted for over 70% of GDP in 2010 but fell back last year as consumers delayed spending in response to the natural disasters.  While consumption has revived somewhat this year, this has largely been brought about by temporary factors such as government subsidies for fuel-efficient automobiles and reconstruction spending.

The pick-up in the first quarter owed little to trade.  Exports to China fell in the quarter by13% year-on-year and to the Eurozone by 10% year-on-year.  While exports to the USA picked up sufficiently to offset the deterioration in demand from China, the recent weakness in the US labour mark

et and political uncertainty in Europe are risks to the future growth of exports.  The deterioration in exports is also in part due to the sustained strength of the yen, which has appreciated by almost 5% since mid-March. 

Aside from a strong currency, there are several other headwinds preventing a return to growth.  Not least of these is the uncertainty surrounding the future of energy generation.  The last of Japan’s remaining nuclear reactors went offline in early May leaving the country without nuclear energy for the first time in 40 years.  This has cast considerable doubt on the outlook for energy policy in Japan and on the economic cost of future industrial activity.  Furthermore, with exports softening and an increasing reliance on imports of expensive fossil fuels to generate replacement power, the trade deficit has widened to an historical high. 

High frequency data are not too encouraging either.  Industrial output, for example, rose by a less than expected 1.0% in March from February and manufacturers said they expected to cut output by 4.0% in May.  The deterioration in the outlook for industry was reinforced by the Markit manufacturing PMI.  The reading for April dropped off slightly from 51.1 in March to 50.7, signalling a marginally slower rate of growth in manufacturing output than the previous month, but consistent with continued, but slow recovery. 

While the pick-up in economy activity in the first quarter was encouraging, we think it is likely that growth will soften throughout the remainder of this year.  We expect domestic demand to be hit by the withdrawal of temporary spending incentives and the global slowdown to continue to hamper external demand.  We have therefore maintained our outlook of around 1.7% growth this year followed by around 2% annual growth throughout 2013 to 2016. 

Signs are accumulating that India’s poor economic performance in 2011 might be rolling over into 2012.  The economy remains dogged by structural issues, hampering its ability to return to high growth rates.  Interventions by authorities do not yet seem to have had the desired effects.  In terms of monetary policy, for example, last month’s interest rate cut may not yet have had much of an impact but based on the indicators highlighted below, the economy appears to be in a worse state.  Furthermore, the current account and fiscal and trade deficits remain at or around historical highs and inflation is back on the rise. 

The rupee has also come under increased pressure in recent weeks.  After a period of very steep depreciation since the beginning of February, the rupee hit an all-time low in May (above Rs 55 to the dollar).  Foreign institutional investors, following anxiety over a widening trade gap and an environment hostile to investment, pulled money out of India in April to the tune of $105 million after average inflows of $3 billion in each of the previous three months. 

Whilst a weaker currency should offer some scope for exporters

to benefit, exports have recently under performed.  In April, growth in exports recovered only some ground against the fall in March, rising 3.2% year-on-year after falling 5.7% the month before. 

Elsewhere, industrial production contracted 3.5% year-on-year in March reversing almost entirely the 4.1% gain in February.  The unexpected fall in output was driven by a 21.2% yearon-year drop in capital goods and manufacturing (electrical machinery manufacturing sank

Thailand bounced back to growth in the first quarter of 2012 after a slump in activity in the fourth quarter due to extensive flooding.  Following a 10.8% quarter-on-quarter decline in GDP in the fourth quarter, economic activity expanded by 11% quarter-on-quarter in the first three months of 2012.  Investment climbed by almost 14% quarter-on-quarter on the back of reconstruction spending.  Growth in exports was similarly impressive, rising by 11.6% quarteron-quarter, as manufacturing production resumed.  We have left our forecast broadly unchanged with growth of 4.7% this year, followed by 6.7% next year. 

Following two quarters in which economic activity contracted, GDP in Taiwan expanded by a seasonally-adjusted 1.1% quarter-on-quarter in the first three months of 2012.  The weak recovery from recession was led by consumer spending which rose 1.5% year-on-year compared with 1.0% in the fourth quarter.  We forecast growth of 2.5% this year, although given Taiwan’s high dependency on exports, weakness overseas may derail the recovery.
